solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Some say Trump is one angry at a court (8)

indicators.note: an angry arrangement is a disturbed one, so the letters are stirred up

annotation.surface: A political jab: critics say the President rages against the judges who rule against him.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole phrase, and 'Some say' keeps it fair: the setter is reporting an opinion, not asserting one. It sounds like a homophone signal, but here it is only part of the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An autocrat rules alone and unchecked, which is what his critics accuse Trump of wanting.

entries.clue: Primate in NHS unit is essentially kaput (3)

indicators.note: the letter from kaput goes inside the NHS unit
the essence of a word is its centre, so take the middle letter

blocks.note: A&E, the accident and emergency department of a hospital
the middle letter of kAPut... the centre of K-A-P-U-T is P

annotation.surface: A hospital department is described as broken at its core.
annotation.walkthrough: A&E is the British name for the emergency room; the ampersand is dropped, leaving AE to hold the P.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: gorillas, chimps and orangutans belong to the primate order alongside monkeys and humans.

entries.clue: Some stiff in gait rowing at gentle pace? (7)

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase that follows are used

annotation.surface: A rower is stiff-legged, so the boat is taken out at an easy pace.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts 'rowing' in a boat; the answer means rowing as in quarrelling (rhymes with 'cow'). A tiff is a small quarrel, so tiffing is rowing at a gentle level, and the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A tiff is a minor quarrel, so tiffing is mild squabbling: rowing turned down low.

entries.clue: Ring that bloke’s taken into church (5)

indicators.note: someone taken into a building ends up inside it, so HIM goes inside the letters for church

blocks.note: that bloke = him; the 's is read as 'is'

annotation.surface: A man is brought into church for a wedding ring.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's in bloke's means 'is', joining HIM to the instruction: that bloke is taken into church.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: church bells and doorbells both sound out, the sense the surface hides behind a wedding band.

entries.clue: Fine to be a part of wild safari romances (7)

indicators.note: F joins the letters being mixed
the letters run wild, out of order

blocks.note: f = fine, as on pencil leads

annotation.surface: An advert: holiday romances on a wild safari sound just fine.
annotation.walkthrough: Fine joins the fodder rather than being a separate chunk: SAFARI plus F is shuffled.
annotation.definitionFit: The word's romantic sense, short for 'love affairs', usually implying something brief or illicit.

entries.clue: Musical composition used in Rastafarianism (4)

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the next word

annotation.surface: A piece of music played in Rastafarian worship.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface points to reggae; the answer is the operatic opposite.
annotation.definitionFit: An aria is a solo song in an opera, a musical composition.

entries.clue: Regret screening Alien on hot train (7)

indicators.note: RUE hides the next pieces inside it
in a down clue, one piece placed on another comes directly before it

blocks.note: RUE = regret, opening around the middle

annotation.surface: Someone regrets watching the film Alien on a sweltering train.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Screening' pretends to mean showing a film, and 'train' pretends to be the railway. A train here is a trail of followers.
annotation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of attendants following an important person, a train.

entries.clue: I’m told a loan must be taken out to get a drink (11)

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of their order and rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone is told they will have to borrow money just to buy a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I'm told' looks like a homophone signal, but it is simply fodder; every letter of it is used.
annotation.definitionFit: Amontillado is a medium-dry sherry, a drink.

entries.clue: Buzzer and foghorn at front create complaint (4)

indicators.note: take just the front letter of foghorn

annotation.surface: A doorbell and a foghorn together make a noise nuisance, prompting a complaint.
annotation.walkthrough: The buzzer is not a gadget but an insect.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang sense: to have a beef with someone is to hold a grievance against them.

entries.clue: Crime Republican admitted to popular splinter group (10)

indicators.note: someone admitted to a club is let in, so R goes inside the word for splinter group

blocks.note: FACTION = splinter group, opening to take R

annotation.surface: A Republican is let into a popular breakaway faction and trouble follows.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Popular' must be read on its own as IN before FACTION, not as describing the group.
annotation.definitionFit: An infraction is a breach of a rule, a minor crime.

entries.clue: Green leader abandoning confusion and commotion (7)

indicators.note: the first letter leaves the word for confusion

annotation.surface: The Green Party's leader walks out amid confusion and commotion.
annotation.walkthrough: Green is the colour, not the party: avocado is a shade of green.
annotation.definitionFit: Avocado is a dull yellowish green, named after the fruit.

entries.clue: One often battered and put down around India (6)

indicators.note: placed around something means surrounding it, so the word for put down wraps round I

blocks.note: PLACE = put down, opening around I
I = India in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Someone beaten and humiliated in India.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Battered' suggests violence; it means coated in batter. Plaice is a flat fish, a staple of British fish and chips.
annotation.definitionFit: Plaice is a fish often fried in batter.

entries.clue: Promiscuous cleric, I hear, is reckless type (5,6)

indicators.note: what follows is how the word sounds

blocks.note: loose = promiscuous, as in loose morals
a canon is a cleric of a cathedral; it sounds like cannon

annotation.surface: A gossip hears that a certain vicar sleeps around and is a menace.
annotation.walkthrough: The homophone covers only the cleric; LOOSE is taken straight.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose cannon is an unpredictable person liable to cause damage.

entries.clue: Eat in or out around noon or not fussy? (8)

indicators.note: the letters are put out of order
the mixed letters go around N

annotation.surface: A lunchtime question: dine in or go out at midday, if you are not choosy?
annotation.walkthrough: The mixed letters wrap around N, in the order INOR-N-ATE. 'Eat in or out' reads as a choice, but 'out' is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Inornate means plain, without ornament, so not fussy.

entries.clue: Do with girls putting away English cakes (8)

indicators.note: GALS put E away inside themselves

blocks.note: to do someone = to con them
GALS = girls, opening to take E

annotation.surface: A party with the girls polishing off the English cakes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Do' looks like a party and 'cakes' looks like food; they are a swindle and a verb meaning sets hard.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that cakes congeals, thickening into a solid mass.

entries.clue: As cares piled up, one man ultimately broke (7)

indicators.note: the cares crash together, jumbled
take the last letter of man
the whole collection breaks up and is reassembled

annotation.surface: Worries mount until a man finally cracks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'As' reads as 'while'; it is the chemical symbol of arsenic.
annotation.definitionFit: A symbol standing for its element: the periodic table abbreviates it As, from its Latin name arsenicum.

entries.clue: A precious metal coating Eastern antique (3-3)

indicators.note: GOLD coats E, wrapping round it

annotation.surface: A gilded antique from the East.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface has 'antique' describing the gilded object; it is the definition on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain adjectival synonym: both describe something that has lasted for a very long time.

entries.clue: American cars or SEATs valets picked up? (6)

blocks.note: sedan is the American word for a saloon car
sedan chairs: seats carried on poles by servants

annotation.surface: Parking valets pick up customers' cars, SEAT being a Spanish car brand.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitalised SEAT makes you think of the Spanish carmaker and a valet parking service; the second sense is the old sedan chair, a seat lifted and carried by footmen.
annotation.definitionFit: A sedan is a saloon car in the US, and a sedan chair was a seat carried on poles.

entries.clue: Cheer up a flipping wearing husband (7)

indicators.note: IN is flipped round to NI

annotation.surface: Cheering up a husband who is wearing something flipping ridiculous.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word, as in 'flipping heck'; here it turns the next word round.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym from the Latin anima, breath or life: to bring life and spirit into a glum person.

entries.clue: Head to barbers to have little off top (4,4)

indicators.note: the head of barbers is its first letter

blocks.note: low = little, as in a low number

annotation.surface: A man goes to the barber's to have a little taken off the top.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top' is slang for kill, not the top of the head; blow away also means kill by shooting.
annotation.definitionFit: To blow someone away is to shoot them dead, and to top someone is to kill them.

entries.clue: Bishop on drugs colony locks up for this? (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, the bishop sits on top of what follows

blocks.note: E = ecstasy, so two Es are drugs
a colony of bees lives in a hive

annotation.surface: A drug-taking bishop is locked up in a penal colony.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Locks up' is not imprisonment but hair piled up: a beehive is a tall 1960s hairdo. The question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A beehive is a hairstyle with the locks piled high on the head.

entries.clue: Draw a model of car and vehicle with no men in it (7)

indicators.note: OR, the men, is removed from the vehicle

blocks.clueFragment: vehicle with no men in it
blocks.note: TRACTOR without OR (other ranks, the men)

annotation.surface: An artist is asked to draw a model car and an empty vehicle.
annotation.walkthrough: OR stands for 'other ranks', soldiers who are not officers, which is why 'men' gives OR.
annotation.definitionFit: To attract is to draw in, as a magnet draws iron.

entries.clue: Cards constituents of a ward delivered (8)

indicators.note: a speech is delivered, so the sound is what counts

blocks.note: the people in a hospital ward

annotation.surface: Get-well cards handed out to the people on a hospital ward.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' looks like the cards being handed over; it means spoken. Patience is the British name for solitaire.
annotation.definitionFit: Patience is a card game for one player, known in America as solitaire.

entries.clue: Chubby? Getting curt digs? Work out! (6)

indicators.note: curt means cut short, so the last letter of HOME goes

blocks.note: digs = home, a British word for lodgings, cut short

annotation.surface: A fitness taunt: overweight and insulted, so off to the gym!
annotation.walkthrough: 'Digs' reads as insults and 'Work out' as exercise. Digs are lodgings; to work out a puzzle is to fathom it.
annotation.definitionFit: Figurative sense of measuring sea depth: getting to the bottom of a problem means understanding it.

entries.clue: Kind of plate covered by food for spread (5)

indicators.note: what is covered by something sits underneath and inside it, so L goes within the word for food

blocks.note: an L-plate, the sign on a British learner driver's car

annotation.surface: A special dish holding food for a buffet spread.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plate' and 'spread' both suggest a meal. An L-plate is the red L a British learner driver must display, and a spread here is a widening, as of flared trousers.
annotation.definitionFit: To flare is to spread out, widening towards the end.

entries.clue: Can’t air act differently in a cold place? (10)

indicators.note: the letters are set out differently

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether you cannot air things out when the room is freezing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Can't' supplies its letters without the apostrophe. The question mark signals that 'a cold place' is understated: it is the coldest place on Earth.
annotation.definitionFit: Antarctica is the coldest continent on Earth.

entries.clue: Those likely to embrace fighting (4)

blocks.note: the limbs that do the hugging
warfare and weapons, as in 'a call to ...'

annotation.surface: People keen to join a fight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Embrace' suggests adopting a cause, as in embracing a fight; it is literal hugging.
annotation.definitionFit: Arms do the embracing, and arms means weapons and warfare, as in 'take up arms'.

entries.clue: Abrupt chap on Yes, Prime Minister (3)

indicators.note: abrupt means cut off, so MAN loses its end
in a down clue, MA sits on Y

annotation.surface: A curt man appearing on the TV sitcom Yes, Prime Minister.
annotation.walkthrough: The sitcom title is split: 'Yes' is wordplay and 'Prime Minister' the definition. Theresa May was UK Prime Minister from 2016 to 2019.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Theresa May led the UK government from 2016 to 2019.

entries.clue: Retrospective study about European poverty (4)

indicators.note: looking backwards, so DEN is read in reverse
the reversed study goes about E

blocks.note: DEN = study, reversed to NED and opening around E

annotation.surface: A retrospective academic study of poverty in Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective study' reads as one academic phrase; the first word is the instruction to reverse the second.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain noun synonym: lacking the necessities of life, as in 'families in ...'.

entries.clue: Bank taking in little coin of late (8)

indicators.note: RELY takes CENT inside it

blocks.note: a cent is a small coin

annotation.surface: A bank has lately started accepting small change.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bank' is not the institution but the verb: to bank on something is to rely on it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain adverbial synonym: both place something in the time just past.
